sections.title: The Four Pillars of OOP in Java — Quick Overview
sections.content:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) organizes code around **objects** — self-contained units that combine data (fields) and behavior (methods). A **class** is the blueprint; an **object** is an instance of that class. Create a `Dog` class with `name` and `breed` as fields and `bark()` and `eat()` as methods — every dog object you create from it gets the same structure.

Java's OOP is built on four core principles: **Encapsulation**, **Inheritance**, **Polymorphism**, and **Abstraction**. Each one solves a specific design problem — they're the rules for how objects protect their data, relate to each other, and hide complexity.

sections.title: Four Pillars at a Glance
sections.content:

blue|Inheritance|~Child acquires parent via extends|IS-A test before using it|no multiple via classes|prefer composition (HAS-A)
emerald|Polymorphism|~One entity, many forms|overloading = compile-time|overriding = runtime|JVM picks by actual object type
violet|Abstraction|~Hide how, show what|abstract class: 0-100%|interface: 100%|design principle, not a keyword

sections.title: Encapsulation: The Class Controls Its Own State
sections.content:
**Encapsulation** means bundling data (fields) and the methods that work on that data together inside a class, and restricting direct access from outside. The fields are the class's private state; the methods are the controlled access points.

Think of it like a medicine capsule — the active ingredients are sealed inside. You interact with the tablet as a whole, not with individual chemicals. A `BankAccount` works the same way: you don't reach in and modify `balance` directly; you call `withdraw()`.

- Declare fields `private`; expose only through public methods
- The key rule: expose **behavior**, not state — `account.withdraw(100)` is right; `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 100)` is not
- The class owns its logic — validation, overdraft checks, and audit logs live inside, invisible to callers
- If `balance` changes from `double` to `BigDecimal`, no caller breaks — they only ever called `withdraw()`

sections.title: Theater: private field, but the caller controls all logic
Real encapsulation: the class owns its invariants
Inheritance: Acquire Properties via IS-A
sections.content:
**Inheritance** lets a child class acquire the properties and methods of a parent class using the `extends` keyword. `Dog extends Animal` — the `Dog` class gets everything `Animal` has (`name`, `age`, `eat()`, `sleep()`) and can add its own (`bark()`) or override existing behavior.

This models an IS-A relationship. A dog **is** an animal. A cat **is** an animal. Unlike a car, which *has* an engine — that's not inheritance, that's composition. The IS-A test is how you decide which to use.

- **IS-A test first**: `Dog IS-A Animal` ✓ → `extends`. `Car HAS-A Engine` ✗ → use composition instead
- Java supports: single, multilevel (`Dog → Animal → Object`), hierarchical (`Dog, Cat → Animal`). Multiple inheritance via classes = **not allowed** (diamond problem)
- Prefer interfaces for multiple inheritance
- Deep hierarchies (4+ levels) = design smell; prefer flat hierarchies + composition

sections.title: Inheritance misused — hierarchy collapses
Composition — behaviors assembled, not inherited
Polymorphism: One Interface, Many Forms
sections.content:
**Polymorphism** means "many forms" — the same method name or interface behaves differently depending on the actual object type. A `Shape` can be a `Circle`, a `Rectangle`, or a `Triangle`. Call `shape.area()` on any of them — you get the right calculation without knowing which shape it is.

A useful real-world frame: a person behaves differently as a father at home, an employee at work, a student in class. Same person — many behaviors depending on context.

- **Compile-time (overloading)**: same method name, different parameters — compiler picks the right version at build time
- **Runtime (overriding)**: `Shape s = new Circle(); s.area()` — JVM picks `Circle`'s version based on the actual object type, not the reference type
- Without it: adding a new type means editing existing code — a growing `if-else` chain for every new variant
- With it: new type = new class, zero existing code touched

sections.title: Without polymorphism — adding ApplePay edits this method
With polymorphism — new type = new class, zero existing code touched
Abstraction: Depend on Contracts, Not Implementations
sections.content:
**Abstraction** means hiding the implementation details and showing only what the user needs. The "how" stays hidden; only the "what" is visible.

You use abstraction every day without thinking about it. A TV remote has a "volume up" button — you don't know the circuit board. An ATM lets you withdraw cash — the banking system behind it is invisible. That's abstraction: you see the interface, not the engine.

- `interface` = 100% abstraction — pure contract, no implementation detail exposed
- `abstract class` = partial abstraction — can have both abstract (no body) and concrete (with body) methods
- The practical daily rule: `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` — declare the interface type, not the concrete class. Swap to `LinkedList` — no caller changes
- The common confusion: `abstract` is a Java keyword; abstraction is a design *principle*. An `interface` achieves full abstraction without the `abstract` keyword at all

sections.title: Declare the interface type — never the concrete class
What Each Pillar Actually Protects You From
sections.content:
| Pillar | The Problem It Solves | Java Mechanism | What Breaks Without It |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Encapsulation** | External code depends on internal structure — any field change breaks callers | `private` fields, methods as the only access path | `int` → `long` field change cascades through every direct accessor |
| **Inheritance** | Shared behavior is copy-pasted — bug fixes need updating in N places | `extends`, `@Override`, `super` | Logging format change requires editing 15 classes instead of one parent |
| **Polymorphism** | Adding a new variant requires editing existing code | Method overriding, interfaces, overloading | New `PaymentMethod` forces editing `processPayment()` and retesting all paths |
| **Abstraction** | Callers coupled to implementation — swapping a library rewrites consumers | Interfaces, `abstract` classes | Replacing MySQL with PostgreSQL means rewriting every service that called it |

They reinforce each other: encapsulation makes polymorphism safe; abstraction guides where inheritance boundaries should be.

sections.title: Where All Four Pillars Converge in One Line
sections.content:
```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();  // all four pillars, one line
```

| Pillar | What it does here |
|---|---|
| **Abstraction** | `List` is the contract — implementation hidden from every caller |
| **Encapsulation** | `ArrayList`'s internal array is inaccessible to callers |
| **Polymorphism** | Any `List` implementation substitutes without changing callers |
| **Inheritance** | `ArrayList` fulfills the `List` contract via `implements` |

`ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` breaks all four — one word change couples every caller to that specific class.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Encapsulation** — `private` fields + behavior methods. Use `withdraw()`, not `setBalance()`.
- **Inheritance** — IS-A via `extends`. No multiple through classes (diamond problem). IS-A test first.
- **Polymorphism** — overloading = compile-time (compiler picks). Overriding = runtime (JVM picks by actual type).
- **Abstraction** — interface = 100%, abstract class = partial. Design *principle*, not the `abstract` keyword.
- **All four in one** — `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>()` uses every pillar simultaneously.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
OOP organizes code around objects — each object combines its data and behavior in one place. In Java, a class is the blueprint and an object is an instance of it. The four principles that define how you design those objects are Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction.

**Encapsulation**
- Keep fields `private` and expose them only through public methods
- The class should own its own logic — `account.withdraw(100)` is encapsulation; `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 100)` is not, because you've moved the logic outside the class
- This also protects you from change — if `balance` moves from `double` to `BigDecimal`, no caller breaks because they never accessed the field directly

**Inheritance**
- A child class acquires the properties and methods of a parent using `extends` — `Dog extends Animal`
- Before using it, ask: is this an IS-A relationship? A dog *is* an animal — that works. A car *has* an engine — that's composition, not inheritance
- Java supports single, multilevel, and hierarchical inheritance. Multiple inheritance through classes isn't allowed because of the diamond problem — use interfaces for that

**Polymorphism**
- One interface, many implementations — the same method call behaves differently depending on the object
- Compile-time: method overloading — same name, different parameters, the compiler picks the right version
- Runtime: method overriding — `Shape s = new Circle(); s.area()` calls Circle's version because the JVM looks at the actual object type, not the reference type

**Abstraction**
- Hide the how, expose the what — like an ATM: you use it without knowing how the banking system works behind it
- An `interface` is 100% abstraction — just the contract, no implementation
- An `abstract class` is partial — it can have some concrete methods along with the abstract ones
- Use an interface when defining a capability like `Flyable`; use an abstract class when there's shared implementation to inherit

The four work as a system, not a checklist. `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` uses all of them — `List` is the abstraction, `ArrayList`'s fields are encapsulated, any List can substitute via polymorphism, and `ArrayList` satisfies the contract through inheritance.

sections.title: Why Java Has Four Access Levels Instead of Just Public and Private
sections.content:
Most developers think in two levels: public or private. They mark fields `private`, add getters and setters, and call it encapsulation. But Java has **four** access levels for a reason, and the two in the middle — default (package-private) and protected — are where the real design decisions happen.

The core idea behind encapsulation isn't hiding data. It's **controlling the surface area of change.** When a class exposes a field or method, every piece of code that uses it becomes a dependency. Change the field type, rename the method, or alter its behavior, and all those dependents break. Access modifiers let you control exactly how wide that scope of change is.

`private` means only this class is affected by changes. `default` (package-private) means your package — your team's internal API — can use it, but nothing outside can depend on it. `protected` extends that to subclasses in other packages. `public` means anyone, anywhere, forever.

The reason most developers skip over default and protected is that IDEs autocomplete `private` and `public`, and the middle two rarely appear in basic examples. But in a codebase with well-structured packages, **the default access level is often the right choice** — it creates boundaries between modules without the ceremony of interfaces. Spring's internal classes use package-private extensively to hide implementation details from the public API while keeping them accessible to related classes in the same package.

sections.content:
amber|private|~This class only|fields, helpers, inner logic|no subclass, no package|default: hide everything
blue|package-private|~Same package only|no keyword — omit modifier|internal API design|Spring internals use this constantly
emerald|protected|~Package + subclasses|same package = yes too|subclasses in other pkgs|strictly wider than package-private
violet|public|~Everyone, everywhere|permanent API surface|removing it = breaking change|every public method = contract

sections.title: The Access Matrix: What Each Modifier Actually Allows
sections.content:
The four access levels form a strict hierarchy from narrowest to widest. The confusion usually lives in the middle two rows — protected is wider than most developers expect.

| Modifier | Same Class | Same Package | Subclass (other package) | Everywhere |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `private` | Yes | No | No | No |
| default (no modifier) | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| `protected` | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| `public` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

The non-obvious detail: **`protected` includes same-package access.** A `protected` method is accessible to every class in the same package — not just subclasses. This means `protected` is strictly wider than default, not a different dimension. Many candidates say protected means "only subclasses," which is wrong.

Another trap: **there is no `default` keyword for access.** You simply omit the modifier. Writing `default` before a field is a syntax error. The term "package-private" is the community name for this level — Java's language spec calls it "default access."

When choosing a modifier, start narrow and widen only with reason. Can anyone outside this class ever need this? If no, `private`. If only classes in this package need it, omit the modifier.

If subclasses in other packages need it, `protected`. Only use `public` for your intentional API surface — once something is public, removing it is a breaking change.

sections.title: The Getter/Setter Trap: Private Fields With Accessors Is Not Encapsulation
sections.content:
Every Java tutorial teaches the same pattern: mark fields `private`, generate getters and setters. It looks right — the field is private, after all. But making a field `private` and adding `getBalance()` and `setBalance()` is not encapsulation. If external code can read and write the field through accessors, the field is effectively public — you've just added a layer of indirection that provides no actual protection.

Real encapsulation exposes behavior, not state. Instead of `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 100)`, the class offers `account.withdraw(100)`. The `withdraw` method validates the amount, checks for overdraft, logs the transaction, and updates the balance internally. The caller doesn't know or care how the balance is stored — it could be an `int`, a `BigDecimal`, or a database call.

This matters in practice because internal representation changes. A `BankAccount` class might start with `private int balance` and later move to `private BigDecimal balance` for precision. With real encapsulation, that change is invisible to callers — `withdraw()` still works. With getter/setter encapsulation, every caller that used `getBalance()` in arithmetic now has a type mismatch.

Lombok's `@Getter` and `@Setter` annotations make this worse by making it effortless to expose every field. Use `@Getter` sparingly — only on fields where external code genuinely needs to read the value — and avoid `@Setter` almost entirely. If a field needs to change, there should be a method that describes why it changes.

Real Encapsulation — Class Owns Its Invariants
Package-Private: The Modifier Senior Engineers Actually Reach For
sections.content:
Every tutorial teaches private and public. Package-private is the one almost never explained, which is exactly why it comes up in interviews about access modifiers.

You get package-private by omitting the modifier entirely — there is no `default` keyword. Writing `default int count` is a syntax error. Any class in the same package can access it; nothing outside the package can. This isn't a forgotten modifier or a lazy shortcut — it's deliberate module boundary design.

The use case: internal implementation classes. If you're building a payment processing package with five internal collaborators, but the only thing external code should ever see is `PaymentProcessor`, you make the four internal classes package-private. External code can't accidentally depend on them. Refactoring them doesn't break callers. Spring Framework does this constantly — if you browse the source of `spring-security`, you'll find dozens of package-private classes orchestrating the filter chain internally, invisible to your application code. Only the public contracts like `SecurityFilterChain` are part of the API.

The decision rule: start `private`, widen to package-private when other classes in the same package need access, widen to `protected` or `public` only when there's a concrete external need. Every public method or field is a contract you maintain forever.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **No modifier = package-private, not `public`** — there is no `default` keyword; you omit the modifier entirely.
- **`protected` includes the same package** — not just subclasses; "protected = only subclasses" is the most common wrong answer.
- **Getters/setters ≠ encapsulation** — `private balance + setBalance()` is effectively public; prefer `account.withdraw(100)`.
- **Start `private`, widen only with reason** — every `public` method is a permanent contract; removing it breaks callers.
- **Lombok `@Setter` on every field bypasses encapsulation** — prefer behavior methods that describe why state changes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Encapsulation is about controlling the surface area of change — not just hiding fields. Every public method or field is a dependency: the wider you expose internals, the more places break when those internals change.

**What encapsulation actually means**
- Private fields plus getters/setters is indirection, not encapsulation — `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 100)` puts all the logic on the caller, with no validation, no overdraft check, no audit log
- Real encapsulation exposes behavior, not state: `account.withdraw(100)` keeps all of that inside the class
- Change `balance` from `double` to `BigDecimal` with real encapsulation — no callers notice, because they called `withdraw()`, never `getBalance()`

**The four access modifiers**
- `private` — class only; no modifier (package-private) — same package; `protected` — same package plus subclasses in other packages; `public` — everyone, permanently
- Interview trap: `protected` ≠ only subclasses — it includes the entire same package, making it strictly wider than package-private
- There is no `default` keyword — you omit the modifier. `default int count` is a syntax error.

**When to reach for each**
- Start `private` — widen only when there's a concrete reason
- Package-private (no modifier): internal classes the same package needs but nothing outside should touch
- Every `public` method is a permanent API contract — once external code depends on it, removing it is a breaking change

Lombok's `@Setter` on every field undoes this entirely. If a field needs to change, there should be a method that describes why — not a setter that just sets.

sections.title: Java Inheritance: IS-A Relationship, super Keyword, and Why It Can Break
sections.content:
Inheritance lets a child class acquire the fields and methods of a parent class using the `extends` keyword. `Dog extends Animal` — every Dog object automatically gets Animal's `name`, `age`, `eat()`, and `sleep()`, and can add its own `bark()` or override what it inherits. The child writes only what's different.

The IS-A relationship is the other half. A Dog **is** an Animal — which means a Dog can be used anywhere an Animal is expected. `Animal a = new Dog()` is valid. Call `a.eat()` and you get Dog's version if it overrides, Animal's version if it doesn't. This substitutability is what makes runtime polymorphism work — the JVM dispatches to the right implementation based on the actual object, not the variable type.

Java supports four inheritance types: **single** (Dog → Animal), **multilevel** (GoldenRetriever → Dog → Animal), **hierarchical** (Dog, Cat, Cow all extend Animal), and **multiple via interfaces** — not classes. Java bans multiple class inheritance because of the diamond problem: if two parents both define `speak()`, the compiler can't choose. Interfaces with `default` methods sidestep this.

The design question — when to use `extends` and when not to — is where most developers need more depth. The IS-A test has a catch: the relationship must hold in **every context**, not just today's. A Square mathematically is a Rectangle, but a `Rectangle` has independent `setWidth()` and `setHeight()`. A caller who sets width to 4 and height to 5 and expects area of 20 gets 25 from a Square. That's the **Liskov Substitution Principle**: if a child can't be substituted for its parent without breaking callers, the inheritance is wrong.

sections.content:
amber|IS-A Test|~Permanent identity check|Dog IS-A Animal ✓|Square IS-A Rectangle? ✗|if it fails → use composition
blue|super()|~Constructor chain|must be first line|compiler inserts if missing|chains up to Object(), then back down
emerald|Override Rules|~Same/wider access|covariant return OK|narrower exceptions only|@Override — always write it
violet|Static Hiding|~Not polymorphism|reference type decides|no vtable dispatch|method hiding, not overriding

sections.title: IS-A in Practice: Types of Inheritance and When the Test Fails
sections.content:
**IS-A** is a substitution test, not just a naming convention. If `Dog extends Animal`, then a Dog must work correctly anywhere an Animal is expected — same contract, same behavioral guarantees. The Dog/Animal case passes easily: Dog inherits `eat()` and `sleep()`, adding `bark()` doesn't break any existing Animal caller.

The four main inheritance types in Java all use relationships that genuinely pass this test:

- **Single**: `Dog extends Animal` — one child, one parent
- **Multilevel**: `Puppy extends Dog extends Animal` — a chain of specialization; each level IS-A its parent
- **Hierarchical**: `Dog`, `Cat`, `Cow` all extend `Animal` — multiple children, one common parent

**Multiple inheritance via classes is not allowed.** If `ClassC extends ClassA, ClassB` and both define `speak()`, the compiler has no rule to pick one — that's the diamond problem. Java solves this through interfaces: a class can implement many interfaces, and since Java 8, `default` methods can coexist because the implementing class can override them explicitly if there's a conflict.

**When IS-A fails — use composition.** Two services sharing validation logic are not in a parent-child relationship; they just have similar code. Making one extend the other ties them together permanently: change the parent's logic, and both children feel it. The alternative is composition — hold the shared behavior as a field (`HAS-A`) rather than inheriting it. You get the same reuse without the structural coupling.

The rule: if you can't honestly say 'B is genuinely a kind of A in every situation it will ever be used,' reach for composition instead.

Method Overriding Rules: What the Compiler Checks and What the JVM Does
sections.content:
Method overriding is how a child provides its own implementation of a method the parent defines. The `@Override` annotation tells the compiler to verify the override is valid. Without it, a typo in the method name silently creates a **new method** instead of overriding — no warning, and the parent's version runs at runtime.

**Same or wider access modifier.** A `protected` parent method can be overridden as `protected` or `public` in the child, never `private`. The reason connects to substitution: any caller that can call the method on the parent must be able to call it on the child. Narrowing access would break that guarantee.

**Covariant return type.** If the parent returns `Animal`, the child can return `Dog` — a more specific type. This was added in Java 5 and is used heavily in builder patterns: `Builder.setName()` can return `Builder`, while `AdvancedBuilder.setName()` returns `AdvancedBuilder` for fluent chaining without casting.

**Checked exceptions can only be narrower.** The child can throw fewer checked exceptions, or more specific subclasses of them, but never a broader exception. Callers catch what the parent's signature declares — if the child introduced something new, existing catch blocks wouldn't cover it.

**Static methods are hidden, not overridden.** If parent and child both define a static method with the same name, the version that runs depends on the **reference type** — not the object type. `Animal a = new Dog(); /* static call via a */` calls Animal's version. No vtable dispatch, no runtime resolution. This is the opposite of polymorphism, and it's a reliable interview trick question.

The practical rule: always write `@Override`. It costs nothing and catches bugs that are otherwise invisible at compile time.

- **`super()` is inserted by the compiler** — omit it and the compiler adds the no-arg; no no-arg parent = compile error.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Inheritance lets a child class acquire the fields and methods of a parent through `extends`. `Dog extends Animal` — Dog gets Animal's properties and can add or override them. The IS-A relationship is the foundation: a Dog is always an Animal, which means a Dog can stand in anywhere an Animal is expected. That substitutability is what makes runtime polymorphism possible — it's not just code sharing.

**IS-A and types**
- Three types: single (`Dog extends Animal`), multilevel (`GoldenRetriever extends Dog extends Animal`), hierarchical (`Dog`, `Cat`, `Cow` all extend `Animal`)
- Multiple via classes is not allowed — diamond problem. Use interfaces instead
- The IS-A test: must hold in every context, not just today's. A Square is mathematically a Rectangle, but a Rectangle caller expects independent width and height — Square breaks that. If the child can't honor the parent's contract, the inheritance is wrong

**The super keyword — three uses**
- `super.field` accesses a parent field shadowed by a same-name child field
- `super.method()` calls the parent's version of an overridden method — used when extending behavior, not replacing it
- `super(args)` calls the parent constructor; must be the first line. Omit it and the compiler inserts `super()` automatically — causes a compile error if the parent has no no-arg constructor

**Method overriding**
- Same or wider access: `protected` can become `public`, never `private`
- Covariant return: child can return a more specific type (`Dog` where parent returns `Animal`)
- Checked exceptions: only narrower — child can't introduce new ones the caller doesn't handle
- Static methods are hidden, not overridden — reference type decides which runs; always write `@Override`

The Liskov Substitution Principle is the interviewer checkpoint. It's the formal name for the IS-A test failing in context — Square-Rectangle is the example everyone expects. Knowing it by name and being able to explain why the code breaks is the answer that separates design-aware from syntax-level.

sections.title: Polymorphism in Java: When the Compiler Decides vs When the JVM Decides
sections.content:
Ask a developer what polymorphism is and they'll say "same method, different behavior." Ask them to explain the difference between compile-time and runtime polymorphism, and you'll immediately see whether they understand the mechanism or just memorized a definition.

The distinction is about **when the decision is made.** Compile-time polymorphism — method overloading — means the compiler looks at the method signature you wrote (name + parameter types) and decides at compile time which method to call. This is a convenience feature: you can have `calculate(int)`, `calculate(double)`, and `calculate(int, int)` in the same class, and the compiler picks the right one based on what you pass.

Runtime polymorphism — method overriding — means the **JVM** decides at execution time. You have a variable typed as `Animal`, but the actual object is a `Dog`. When you call `animal.speak()`, the JVM looks at the real object type, finds `Dog`'s version of `speak()`, and calls that. The compiler can't know which version will run because the object could be created dynamically — from a factory, from a database, from user input.

This runtime decision is what makes polymorphism powerful. It's why you can write `List<Shape> shapes` and call `shape.draw()` on each one without knowing or caring whether it's a `Circle`, `Rectangle`, or `Triangle`. The code works with shapes that don't exist yet — shapes you'll add next month.

sections.title: Compile-Time vs Runtime: When the Decision Happens and Why It Matters
sections.content:
The two forms of polymorphism differ in mechanism, timing, and purpose. The table makes the distinction concrete.

| Aspect | Compile-Time (Overloading) | Runtime (Overriding) |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Same method name, different parameter lists | Same method signature in parent and child |
| Decided by | Compiler, based on declared parameter types | JVM, based on actual object type at runtime |
| Which type matters | **Reference type** (declared type of variable) | **Object type** (actual instance created with `new`) |
| Keyword | None — just define multiple methods | `@Override` annotation (recommended) |
| Can cross classes | No — all overloads must be in the same class | Yes — parent method overridden in child class |
| Return type | Can differ freely | Must be same or covariant (more specific) |
| Access modifier | Can differ freely | Must be same or wider |

The row that trips people up: **which type matters.** With overloading, if you pass a `Dog` to a method that accepts `Animal`, the compiler resolves using the declared parameter type. With overriding, `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` calls `Dog.speak()` because the JVM checks the actual object. This is **dynamic method dispatch** — the JVM uses a vtable (virtual method table) to look up the correct implementation at runtime.

The practical consequence: overloading is just syntactic convenience. Overriding is the mechanism that enables writing code against interfaces and abstract types — the foundation of pluggable architecture.

sections.title: Method Overloading: When the Compiler Makes the Call
Method Overriding: When the JVM Makes the Call at Runtime
sections.content:
Method overriding is resolved at runtime by the JVM, not the compiler. The compiler only verifies that the override is valid — same signature, compatible return type and exceptions. The actual dispatch happens when the method is called on a live object.

The mechanism is the **vtable** (virtual method table). Every class has one — a lookup table mapping method signatures to their concrete implementations. When you call `animal.speak()`, the JVM doesn't go to `Animal`'s `speak()`. It checks the actual object's class, looks up `speak()` in that class's vtable, and calls whatever implementation it finds there.

This is why runtime polymorphism is architecturally powerful. You can write code against the `Animal` interface without knowing which specific animal it is. When you add a new animal type next year, existing code works — no modifications, no recompilation of the callers.

One edge to know for interviews: **private methods can't be overridden.** They aren't in the vtable — they're resolved at compile time to the declaring class. If a parent's method calls a private helper and a child defines the same private method, the parent's method always calls the parent's version. The child's version is invisible to it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Compile-time = overloading, runtime = overriding** — compiler resolves by parameter types; JVM resolves by actual object type.
- **Reference type picks overload; object type picks override** — `Animal a = new Dog()` picks the `Animal` overload, calls `Dog.speak()`.
- **Dynamic dispatch uses a vtable** — per-class virtual method table; method calls look up the real object's entry at runtime.
- **Static methods are hidden, not overridden** — reference type decides which runs, not the object type.
- **Overloading = convenience, overriding = architecture** — overriding is the mechanism behind every pluggable design in Java.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Polymorphism in Java means the same method call can produce different behavior depending on the object it's called on. Java achieves this two ways: overloading at compile time, and overriding at runtime. Most of what interviewers call "polymorphism" refers to the runtime kind — the mechanism that makes interface-based design actually work.

**Compile-time polymorphism — overloading:**
- Overloading lets you define multiple methods with the same name but different parameter types — the compiler resolves which version to call based on the declared argument types at the call site
- The key point is that the reference type decides, not the actual object: passing `Animal a = new Dog()` to an overloaded method runs the `Animal` version, because the compiler locked in its choice before the program ran
- Overloading is a naming convenience — it keeps your API clean by letting you write `draw(Circle)` and `draw(Rectangle)` instead of two different method names; it doesn't provide architectural flexibility

**Runtime polymorphism — overriding:**
- When you call an overridden method, the JVM uses a per-class virtual method table (vtable) to dispatch to the actual object's implementation — not the reference type's version
- `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak()` calls `Dog.speak()` — the JVM checks Dog's vtable at execution time, even though the reference is declared as `Animal`
- This is what makes `List<Shape>` work: you iterate and call `shape.draw()` on each element, and the JVM routes to `Circle.draw()`, `Rectangle.draw()`, or whatever the real object is — no `instanceof` checks needed

**The static method trap:**
- Static methods are hidden, not overridden — they bypass the vtable entirely, so the declared reference type decides which version runs, not the actual object
- This is the standard interview trick: both parent and child define `static void display()` — calling it via an `Animal` reference always runs `Animal.display()` even when the object is a `Dog`; the object type is irrelevant

I recommend writing `@Override` on every intended override — without it, a mistyped method signature silently creates a new method or hides a static method instead of overriding, and the compiler gives no warning.

sections.title: The Decision Java 8 Made Harder: When 'Use an Interface' Stopped Being Obvious
sections.content:
Before Java 8, the choice was simple: need shared method implementations, use an abstract class; need a pure contract, use an interface.

Then Java 8 added **default methods** to interfaces, and the line blurred.

Now interfaces can have method bodies, static methods, and even private helper methods (Java 9+). So the question shifts from "do I need method implementations?" to something more fundamental: **am I defining what something IS, or what something CAN DO?**

An abstract class represents **identity** — a shared base that says "all subclasses are fundamentally this thing." `Animal` is an abstract class because `Dog` and `Cat` are animals at their core. They share state (name, age), behavior (eat, sleep), and a common identity.

An interface represents **capability** — a contract that says "this thing can do X." `Comparable`, `Serializable`, `Runnable` don't describe what something is. They describe something it can do.

A `Dog` might be `Comparable` and `Serializable`, but those aren't part of its identity.

The practical consequence of getting this wrong shows up when requirements change. If you made `Flyable` an abstract class, you can't have a `Duck` that's both an `Animal` and `Flyable` — Java has single inheritance. But if `Flyable` is an interface, a `Duck extends Animal implements Flyable` works perfectly. **Interfaces compose. Abstract classes don't.**

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface: The Complete Decision Matrix
sections.content:
The syntax differences matter less than the design implications. This table covers both.

| Aspect | Abstract Class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Inheritance | Single — `extends` one class only | Multiple — `implements` many interfaces |
| State (fields) | Instance fields, constructors | Constants only (`public static final`) |
| Method bodies | Always allowed | `default` methods (Java 8+), `private` (Java 9+) |
| Access modifiers | Any — `private`, `protected`, package | `public` only (methods are implicitly public) |
| Constructors | Yes — called via `super()` chain | No constructors |
| Design intent | IS-A identity — "this is fundamentally a..." | CAN-DO capability — "this can..." |
| Evolution | Adding abstract methods breaks all subclasses | Adding default methods is backward-compatible |

The evolution row is critical in large codebases. If you add a new abstract method to an abstract class, **every subclass must implement it immediately** — a breaking change across the codebase. Adding a `default` method to an interface is backward-compatible — existing implementations keep working. This is exactly why Java added default methods: to evolve `Collection` and `Iterable` without breaking every class that implemented them.

sections.title: The Decision Rule: Start With an Interface, Reach for Abstract Class Only When You Must
sections.content:
The interface is the default choice in modern Java. Reach for it whenever you're defining a contract or capability that multiple unrelated classes might implement — when callers should depend on an abstraction, not a specific type. The fact that a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one abstract class makes interfaces strictly more composable. `Duck implements Animal, Flyable, Serializable` is valid; inheriting all three is impossible.

Reach for an abstract class only when you need something interfaces still can't provide: shared instance state across subclasses, constructors or initialization logic, or non-public methods in the base type. The template method pattern is the classic use case — an abstract parent defines an algorithm skeleton and declares certain steps `abstract`, forcing subclasses to fill them in while sharing the orchestration logic and any state it depends on.

The evolution consideration is underrated in practice. If you add a new abstract method to an abstract class, every subclass must implement it immediately — a breaking change across the codebase. Adding a `default` method to an interface is backward-compatible; existing implementations keep working unchanged. This is exactly the route Java took when adding `forEach`, `stream`, and `removeIf` to `Collection` in Java 8 without breaking every existing implementation. If you find yourself writing an abstract class, ask whether the shared behavior could live in a `default` method or a composed helper instead — if it can, the interface gives you more flexibility with no trade-off.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Abstraction in Java means hiding the implementation details and exposing only what the caller needs to work with. Java provides two mechanisms for this: interfaces, which define a pure contract with no implementation, and abstract classes, which allow a mix of abstract methods and concrete shared behavior. The distinction between them matters most when designing extensible systems.

**Interface — pure contract:**
- An interface defines what an object can do, not what it is — `Comparable`, `Serializable`, `Runnable` describe capabilities that any class can gain regardless of its inheritance hierarchy
- A class can implement many interfaces, which is how Java compensates for the lack of multiple inheritance — behavior composes horizontally through interfaces
- Since Java 8, interfaces can carry `default` method implementations — this was how `Collection.stream()` was added to millions of existing codebases without breaking anything

**Abstract class — shared implementation:**
- An abstract class makes sense when subclasses share mutable state (instance fields), initialization logic, or non-public helper methods that shouldn't be in an interface
- The template method pattern is the canonical use case: the abstract class defines the algorithm skeleton with abstract steps, and subclasses fill in the specific steps
- `Animal` as an abstract class works because `Dog` and `Cat` genuinely share `name`, `age`, and common behavior — it's an IS-A identity, not just a capability

**The Java 8 shift:**
- Before Java 8, "do I need a method implementation?" was the deciding question — that answer always pointed to abstract classes
- After Java 8, the real question is: do you need shared **state** (instance fields) or **constructors**? Only abstract classes can have those; interfaces can now have method bodies
- Adding a new `default` method to an interface is backward-compatible; adding a new `abstract` method to an abstract class immediately breaks every existing subclass

I recommend interfaces as the default in modern Java; reach for abstract classes only when you genuinely need shared mutable state or constructor logic that subclasses must run.

sections.title: The Fragile Base Class Problem: Why Inheritance Breaks When Code Evolves
sections.content:
Most developers reach for `extends` when they see shared code between two classes. Two services both need logging and validation? Make a `BaseService` and inherit from it. This feels clean for about three months — then the base class starts breaking its children.

The problem is called the **fragile base class problem**, and it's the reason the Gang of Four wrote "favor composition over inheritance" in 1994. When you inherit, your subclass is permanently coupled to every implementation detail of the parent. Change a method's behavior in the parent, and every child inherits that change — even if the change breaks assumptions the child was relying on.

Java's own standard library has a famous example. `java.util.Stack` extends `Vector`. That means `Stack` inherits `insertElementAt()`, which lets you insert an element in the middle — violating the entire contract of a stack. The Java team couldn't fix this without breaking backward compatibility, so the Javadoc for `Stack` literally says "A more complete and consistent set of LIFO stack operations is provided by the `Deque` interface."

**Composition** avoids this by holding a reference to the shared behavior instead of inheriting it. Your class **uses** the behavior but isn't **coupled** to its internal implementation. When the shared behavior changes, your class interacts through a stable interface — the internal change is invisible.

sections.title: The Fragile Base Class Trap: When Inheritance for Code Reuse Goes Wrong
sections.content:
Inheritance feels like the natural solution when two classes share code. You see 40% overlap between `ReportService` and `InvoiceService`, so you create a `BaseDocumentService` and extend both from it. For a while this works. Then the requirements diverge. `ReportService` needs a different validation approach. `InvoiceService` needs to add retry logic. Every change to `BaseDocumentService` requires checking what it breaks in both children.

This is the fragile base class problem. The symptom: changing a method in the parent requires reading every child to understand the impact. The cause: the child depends not just on the parent's interface, but on every implementation detail — which methods call which, what order things run, which fields are mutated when. That internal coupling is invisible until someone makes a change.

Java's own standard library documents the consequence. `Stack extends Vector` was written in 1996. `Stack` inherits `insertElementAt()`, `removeElementAt()`, `indexOf()` — none of which make sense on a stack. The Javadoc literally says "a more complete and consistent set of LIFO stack operations is provided by the `Deque` interface." The Java team can't fix it without breaking every program that imports `java.util.Stack`.

sections.title: The Real Cost: What Happens Over 12 Months of Development
sections.content:
The trade-off between inheritance and composition isn't about syntax — it's about what happens when the codebase grows and requirements change over time.

| Dimension | Inheritance (`extends`) | Composition (field reference) |
|---|---|---|
| Coupling | Permanent, structural — child depends on parent's implementation details | Loose — depends on interface, not implementation |
| Multiple behaviors | One parent only (Java's single inheritance) | Combine any number of composed objects |
| Changing behavior at runtime | Fixed at compile time | Swap implementations via strategy/delegate pattern |
| Base class changes | Ripple into all children, can break silently | Contained behind interface boundary |
| Testing | Must test with parent's behavior included | Mock the composed dependency independently |
| Adding a cross-cutting concern | Forces everything into one hierarchy | Inject a new dependency without restructuring |

The **testing row is underrated**. When you unit-test a class that extends `BaseService`, you're also testing every method `BaseService` provides — the test scope is wider than the class you wrote. With composition, you mock the dependency and test only your class's logic.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Composition and inheritance are two fundamental approaches to code reuse and behavioral flexibility in Java. Inheritance uses `extends` to acquire a parent's implementation — but it also creates a permanent coupling to every implementation detail of that parent. Composition instead holds behavior through interface references, which makes it loosely coupled, swappable at runtime, and straightforward to test.

**The fragile base class problem:**
- When a child class `extends` a parent, it silently inherits every dependency and behavior of that parent — change the parent's internals and children break, often in ways that aren't immediately obvious
- Java's `Stack extends Vector` is the canonical mistake: Stack inherited `insertElementAt()` and `removeElementAt()`, which permanently violate the LIFO contract — callers can insert at position 3 of a "stack"
- The Javadoc still says to use `Deque` instead; the class can't be fixed without breaking backward compatibility — that's how permanent the coupling is

**Why composition is more flexible:**
- Composition holds behavior via an interface reference — `ReportGenerator` has a `ReportFormatter` field — which means you can inject `PdfFormatter`, `CsvFormatter`, or `ExcelFormatter` without creating a new subclass for each
- Adding new capabilities (logging, retry, auditing) means injecting more collaborators as separate fields, not extending deeper into a class hierarchy
- Composed dependencies can be mocked in isolation — unit testing a class that `extends` requires testing all parent behavior too; composition lets you test each piece independently

**When inheritance is the right choice:**
- Genuine IS-A with a permanent relationship that will never need swapping: `Dog extends Animal` is appropriate if `Dog` really is an Animal in every context
- Template method pattern: the parent defines the algorithm skeleton and subclasses fill in well-defined abstract steps — a clean use of inheritance with clear boundaries

I recommend defaulting to composition. Reach for inheritance only when the IS-A relationship is genuine and permanent, and behavior never needs to be swapped at runtime.

sections.title: The Question Behind the Question: Who Owns the Object's Lifecycle?
sections.content:
Think of a car. The **engine** is composition — the car created it, the car owns it, and when the car is scrapped, the engine goes with it. The **driver** is aggregation — the driver exists independently, gets assigned to the car, and continues to exist after the car is gone. The car's relationship with the **road** is association — they interact but neither owns or manages the other.

These three terms describe the same thing in different strengths: **how tightly one object's lifecycle is bound to another's.** In Java, there's no keyword for any of them — no `aggregates` or `composes` modifier. The distinction lives entirely in how you write the code: who calls `new`, who holds the reference, and what happens when the container object is garbage collected.

The reason interviewers ask this isn't to test UML knowledge. It's to see whether you think about **object ownership** when designing classes. A class that creates its dependencies internally (composition) is tightly coupled — you can't test it without the real dependency. A class that receives its dependencies (aggregation) is loosely coupled — you can inject mocks. This distinction is the foundation of dependency injection, and understanding it at the relationship level makes DI patterns intuitive rather than magical.

The three relationships form a spectrum from loosest to tightest coupling. The lifecycle column is what actually matters in code.

|---|---|---|---|
| Relationship strength | Weakest — uses | Medium — has-a (shared) | Strongest — has-a (exclusive) |

| Real-world analogy | Teacher ↔ Student | Department → Professor | House → Room |

The code distinction is concrete. In aggregation, the dependent object is **passed in** — it existed before and will exist after. In composition, the dependent object is **created inside** the owner — its lifecycle is entirely controlled.

This maps directly to Spring's dependency injection model. When Spring injects a bean via `@Autowired`, that's **aggregation** — the bean exists in the container independently, and multiple classes can share it. When you define an inner bean in XML config or create an object with `new` inside a method, that's **composition** — the object lives and dies with its creator.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Association, aggregation, and composition describe three types of relationships between objects in object-oriented design — they differ in how strongly one object's lifecycle is tied to another's. There is no special Java syntax for any of them; the distinction lives entirely in who creates the object and who holds the reference.

**Composition — owns and creates:**
- Composition is the tightest binding: the owner creates the part using `new` directly in its constructor — `Car` does `this.engine = new Engine()`, meaning the car's construction directly causes the engine's creation
- The part cannot exist independently — when `Car` is garbage-collected with no other references to its engine, the engine is collected too; this maps to `CASCADE DELETE` in a relational database
- A real giveaway: if you can't create the part without creating the owner first, it's composition

**Aggregation — uses but doesn't own:**
- Aggregation is a looser relationship: the part is constructed elsewhere and passed in — `Department(List<Professor> professors)` receives professors that were created independently
- Professors continue to exist after the department is dissolved — they were never owned by the department, just referenced; the department going away doesn't trigger their destruction
- Spring `@Autowired` is always aggregation — the beans are created and managed by the container, not by the class that receives them

**Association — interacts without ownership:**
- Association is the loosest: two objects interact but neither creates nor manages the other's lifecycle; the relationship exists only for the duration of an interaction
- This shows up as a method parameter or a temporary local reference — a `Teacher` who grades a `Student` doesn't create the student and doesn't hold a permanent field reference

I recommend the lifecycle test when uncertain: if you delete the parent and the child should disappear with it, that is composition. If the child continues to exist independently, that is aggregation.

sections.title: Two References to the Same Object: Why Java Needs Both this and super
sections.content:
`this` and `super` both point to the current object — but they access different parts of it. `this` refers to the current class's view: its own fields, its own methods, its own constructors. `super` refers to the **parent class's view** of the same object: the parent's fields, the parent's method implementations, the parent's constructors.

The key insight most developers miss is that `super` doesn't reference a separate object. There's only one object in memory. `super` is a way to explicitly reach the parent's version of something when the child has hidden or overridden it. Without `super`, once you override a method, the parent's implementation becomes unreachable from the child.

Both keywords serve **two distinct roles** that are worth separating. As **references** (`this.field`, `super.method()`), they disambiguate which version of a field or method you mean. As **constructor calls** (`this(args)`, `super(args)`), they chain constructors — `this()` calls another constructor in the same class, `super()` calls the parent's constructor. The constructor form must be the first statement, which means `this()` and `super()` can never appear in the same constructor — a rule that makes sense once you realize both are trying to be the first thing that initializes the object.

The comparison is straightforward once you see them as two lenses on the same object instance.

| Usage | `this` | `super` |

| Field access | `this.name` — current class's field (or hides parent's) | `super.name` — parent's field when child has a field with the same name |

The **implicit `super()` rule** catches developers off guard. If you don't explicitly write `this()` or `super(...)` as the first line of any constructor, the compiler silently inserts `super()` — the no-argument version. If the parent class doesn't have a no-arg constructor, you get a compile error that seems to come from nowhere, because the `super()` call is invisible in your source code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`this()` and `super()` are mutually exclusive** — both must be the first statement; compiler inserts `super()` silently if you write neither.
- **`super` is the parent layer of the same object** — no separate parent object in memory; `super.method()` uses the parent's vtable entry.
- **`this()` chains constructors within a class** — delegate shorter constructors to the full one; every chain ends in `super()`.
- **`super.field` bypasses field hiding** — field resolution uses reference type, unlike method overriding which uses object type.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In Java, `this` and `super` are both references to the same object in memory — they just give you access to different layers of it. `this` is the current class's view of the object; `super` reaches through to what the parent class defined. Knowing both their roles as references and their special constructor forms is essential because the constructor rules cause some of Java's most confusing compile errors.

**`this` — current class reference:**
- `this.name` is the classic use: disambiguating an instance field from a constructor or method parameter that has the same name — without it, `name = name` assigns the parameter to itself and the instance field stays at its default value
- `this.method()` explicitly invokes a method on the current object — occasionally used when calling interface default methods to pick between multiple defaults
- `this(args)` inside a constructor delegates to a sibling constructor in the same class — the telescoping pattern that avoids duplicating validation and default-value logic across multiple constructors

**`super` — parent layer reference:**
- `super.method()` calls the parent's version of a method the child has overridden — typically used when the child wants to extend rather than replace the parent's behavior, such as `super.draw()` followed by adding a highlight
- `super.field` accesses a parent field being hidden by a child field of the same name — note that field resolution uses reference type, unlike method dispatch
- `super(args)` initializes the parent from a child constructor and must be the first statement; if you omit it entirely, the compiler invisibly inserts `super()` — this causes a compile error on a line you never wrote when the parent has no no-arg constructor

**The mutual exclusion rule:**
- `this()` and `super()` cannot both appear in the same constructor — each constructor calls exactly one; the compiler inserts `super()` if you call neither
- A `this()` chain must eventually reach a constructor that calls `super()` — otherwise the parent would never be initialized

I recommend always writing `super(args)` explicitly when the parent requires constructor arguments — the invisible no-arg insertion is the source of one of Java's most misleading error messages.

sections.title: Why Every Object Starts as an Object: The Constructor Chain You Never See
sections.content:
When you write `new Dog("Rex")`, you might think only the `Dog` constructor runs. In reality, Java executes a **chain of constructors** climbing all the way to `java.lang.Object` before your `Dog` constructor body even begins.

This happens because every class extends something — even if you don't write `extends`, Java implicitly extends `Object`. And every constructor must initialize the parent before initializing itself. The mechanism is **constructor chaining**: each constructor calls either `this()` (another constructor in the same class) or `super()` (a constructor in the parent class) as its very first action.

`this()` is a **DRY tool** — it lets you delegate from simpler constructors to more complete ones within the same class, avoiding duplicated initialization logic. A no-arg constructor calls `this(defaultName, defaultAge)` which does the real work.

`super()` is a **structural requirement** — the parent's state must be initialized before the child can safely use inherited fields or methods. The compiler enforces this by requiring `super()` or `this()` as the first statement. If you write neither, it inserts `super()` for you.

The chain always terminates at `Object()`. No matter how deep your hierarchy, every `new` call triggers a cascade: `Dog()` → `Animal()` → `Object()` → then back down through each constructor body. Understanding this chain explains initialization bugs, the rules about what can appear before `super()`, and why circular `this()` calls are a compile error.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Constructor chaining is the rule that every Java constructor must call either `this()` (a sibling constructor in the same class) or `super()` (the parent constructor) as its very first action. Write neither, and the compiler inserts `super()` automatically. This means every `new Dog("Rex")` silently triggers a chain all the way up to `Object()` before a single line of Dog's body executes.

**`this()` — the DRY constructor:**
- The telescoping pattern uses `this()` to build a hierarchy of constructors — the no-arg constructor delegates to the one-arg, which delegates to the full constructor where all the validation and defaults live
- Adding a new parameter later means touching only the full constructor — the shorter delegating constructors keep working automatically without any changes
- Every `this()` chain must eventually terminate in a constructor that calls `super()`; otherwise the parent would never be initialized

**`super()` — the initialization requirement:**
- The parent's fields must be fully set up before the child can safely use any inherited state — this is why the parent constructor always runs before the child's body
- When you omit `super()`, the compiler inserts `super()` automatically — if the parent has no no-arg constructor, you get a compile error on a line you never wrote, pointing at the child class, not the parent
- Write `super(args)` explicitly when the parent requires arguments; it documents the relationship and prevents surprises

**Initialization order:**
- Static initializer blocks run once when the class is first loaded, before any instance is created
- Then: parent instance initializers and parent constructor body execute fully
- Then: child instance initializers and child constructor body execute
- The gotcha interviewers test: if a parent constructor calls an overridden method, the child's override runs during parent construction — but the child's fields haven't been initialized yet, so they're at their zero defaults

I recommend `this()` telescoping to centralize defaults and validation, and switching to the Builder pattern when the number of constructor parameters exceeds four or five.

sections.title: The Methods Every Java Object Inherits — and the Contract Most Developers Break
sections.content:
Every class in Java extends `Object`, which means every object you create inherits eleven methods. Interviewers care about five of them — `toString()`, `hashCode()`, `equals()`, `clone()`, and `finalize()` — because each one has a contract that's easy to violate and hard to debug when you do.

The one that causes the most real-world bugs is the **equals/hashCode contract**: if two objects are equal according to `equals()`, they must return the same `hashCode()`. Break this, and `HashMap` silently loses your data — `put()` stores the entry in one bucket based on hashCode, but `get()` with an equal key looks in a different bucket and returns `null`. No exception, no warning, just missing data.

`toString()` is the simplest — override it for debugging. The default `ClassName@hexHashCode` is useless in logs. `clone()` looks simple but is fundamentally flawed — it bypasses constructors, returns `Object`, and performs a shallow copy that shares mutable internal state. `finalize()` was Java's attempt at destructor semantics and was deprecated in Java 9 because it introduced unpredictable delays, resurrection bugs, and GC overhead. Modern Java uses `try-with-resources` and `Cleaner` instead.

sections.title: Five Methods, Five Different Contracts
sections.content:
Each method has a specific purpose and a specific set of rules. The table separates what each method does from what goes wrong when you use it incorrectly.

| Method | Purpose | Default behavior | Override correctly | Common trap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `toString()` | Human-readable representation | `ClassName@1a2b3c` (class + hex hashCode) | Include meaningful fields | Forgetting to override — useless log output |
| `hashCode()` | Bucket placement in hash collections | Memory-address-based integer | Must agree with `equals()` | Overriding `equals()` without overriding `hashCode()` — HashMap breaks silently |
| `equals()` | Logical equality | Reference equality (`==`) | Reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, null-safe | Using `==` for field comparison instead of `equals()` on object fields |
| `clone()` | Copy the object | Shallow copy via `Cloneable` marker | Implement `Cloneable`, cast return, deep-copy mutables | Shallow copy shares internal arrays/lists — modifying the clone mutates the original |
| `finalize()` | Cleanup before GC | No-op | Don't override — deprecated since Java 9, removed in Java 18 | Relying on it for resource cleanup — GC timing is unpredictable, may never run |

The **equals/hashCode pair** is the one interviewers probe most. The contract has five properties for `equals()` — reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and `x.equals(null)` returns `false` — but the **one that actually causes production bugs** is the hashCode agreement rule. Java `record` types solve this entirely: they auto-generate `equals()` and `hashCode()` from all component fields, eliminating the most common source of this bug.

sections.title: The equals/hashCode Contract — What Breaks When You Violate It
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`equals()` without `hashCode()` silently loses HashMap data** — `put()` and `get()` hash to different buckets; records fix this automatically.
- **Use `Objects.hash(field1, field2)` with the same fields as `equals()`** — Java records auto-generate both from all components.
- **`clone()` bypasses constructors and is shallow** — mutable internals are shared; use copy constructors instead.
- **`finalize()` — deprecated Java 9, removed Java 18** — unpredictable GC timing; replace with `try-with-resources`.
- **`equals()` contract: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, null-safe** — symmetric breaks most often in class hierarchies.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Every Java class inherits from `Object`. The five methods interviewers focus on are `toString()`, `equals()`, `hashCode()`, `clone()`, and `finalize()`.

**equals/hashCode — the contract that causes production bugs**
- Override `equals()` without `hashCode()` and HashMap silently loses data: `put()` stores in one bucket, `get()` with a logically equal key looks in a different bucket, returns `null`
- Fix: always override both together using the same fields; `Objects.hash(name, age)` is the standard pattern
- Use a `record` when possible — it generates both correctly from all components automatically

**toString()**
- Override it so logs show `Person{name=Alice, age=30}` instead of `Person@1a2b3c`
- Lombok `@ToString` or records handle this automatically

**clone() and finalize() — avoid both**
- `clone()` bypasses constructors, returns `Object` requiring a cast, and shares mutable internals; use copy constructors
- `finalize()` was deprecated in Java 9 and removed in Java 18 — unpredictable GC timing, potential object resurrection; use `try-with-resources` for cleanup

I recommend using Java records for any class used as a map key — they generate correct `equals()` and `hashCode()` automatically, eliminating the most common source of silent data loss.

sections.title: The Bug You Won't See Until Production: Shared References After Copy
sections.content:
Shallow copy and deep copy differ in one thing: what happens to the objects inside your object. A shallow copy duplicates the container but **shares the internal references** — both the original and copy point to the same nested objects in memory. A deep copy duplicates the entire object graph recursively, creating a completely independent clone where no reference is shared.

The problem with shallow copy isn't obvious in tests. Two objects look independent — they have different identities, and assigning new values to primitive or immutable fields works fine because those are either copied by value or can't be mutated anyway. The bug appears only when you mutate a mutable internal object through one reference and discover it changed in the other. Add an item to the copy's `ArrayList`, and it appears in the original's list too.

This is the class of bug that **passes unit tests and fails in production** because tests rarely create a copy and then independently mutate both objects over time. The fix isn't always deep copy — often it's designing with immutable internals so sharing becomes harmless.

sections.title: Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy: What Gets Duplicated
sections.content:
The distinction is purely about **reference depth** — how many levels of the object graph get their own new instances.

| Aspect | Shallow Copy | Deep Copy |
|---|---|---|
| Primitives (`int`, `double`) | Copied by value (independent) | Copied by value (independent) |
| Immutable objects (`String`, `Integer`) | Shared safely — can't be mutated | Shared safely — can't be mutated |
| Mutable objects (`List`, `Date`, custom classes) | Shared reference — modification affects both | New independent instance — modification is isolated |
| Default `clone()` behavior | Shallow — copies fields but not nested objects | Not provided — you must implement recursively |
| Performance | Fast — one level of field copy | Slower — traverses entire object graph |
| Correctness risk | High for mutable internals — silent cross-contamination | Safe — fully independent copy |

The critical insight: **immutable fields don't need deep copying**. A `String` field in a shallow copy is perfectly safe because nobody can mutate the `String` through either reference. The danger is exclusively mutable internal state — `ArrayList`, `Date`, arrays, or any custom class with setters. If all your internal state is immutable, shallow and deep copy are equivalent.

sections.title: How to Actually Copy Objects in Practice
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`clone()` is shallow by default** — mutable fields share references; mutating through the clone silently mutates the original.
- **Immutable fields never need deep copying** — `String`, `Integer`, `LocalDate` can't be mutated; only mutable internals require deep copy.
- **`Arrays.copyOf()` is shallow for object arrays** — new array container, same element references.
- **Copy constructors over `clone()`** — explicit, type-safe, no `Cloneable` required, per-field control.
- **Serialization-based deep copy handles arbitrary nesting** — slow and requires `Serializable`, but no manual recursive copy logic.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Copying an object in Java is not the same as duplicating it — a shallow copy creates a new container but shares references to any mutable objects inside it, while a deep copy recursively creates independent instances of everything in the object graph.

**Shallow copy — where the bug hides**
- Primitives and immutable fields (`String`, `Integer`, `LocalDate`) are safe — they're copied by value or can't be mutated
- Mutable internals are the danger: shallow-copy an `Order` with an `ArrayList<Item>` and both the original and copy share the same list
- Add an item through the copy — it appears in the original with no exception, just silent cross-contamination

**Deep copy — options and trade-offs**
- Copy constructor: `new Order(original)` — explicit, type-safe, per-field control over what needs deep copying
- `new ArrayList<>(original.items)` creates a new list; if `Item` is mutable, you need to copy those too
- Serialization-based: serialize to bytes and deserialize — handles arbitrary nesting, but slow and requires `Serializable`

**The better answer is often immutability**
- If internals are immutable, sharing references is harmless — the shallow vs deep distinction becomes irrelevant
- Defensive copies in constructors protect immutable classes from callers passing mutable objects in

**Defensive copies in constructors:**
- Use `List.copyOf(tags)` in constructors for immutable classes — callers passing a mutable list can't mutate your internal state

I recommend copy constructors over `clone()`, and `List.copyOf()` for defensive copies in constructors.

sections.title: Enums Are Classes — The Feature Most Java Developers Underuse
sections.content:
In most languages, enums are just named integers. Java took a fundamentally different approach: **every enum is a full class** that extends `java.lang.Enum`. Each enum constant is a singleton instance of that class, created once during class loading and never again.

This means enums can have fields, constructors, methods, and implement interfaces — just like any other class. The constructor is implicitly `private` (you can't create enum instances with `new`), and the set of instances is fixed at compile time. These two constraints — private construction and a fixed instance set — give enums properties that are hard to achieve any other way.

Enums are **inherently thread-safe** because the JVM guarantees class loading happens once, in a thread-safe manner. They're **serialization-safe** because deserialization returns the existing singleton rather than creating a new instance — the duplicate-instance problem that plagues `Serializable` classes doesn't exist for enums. And they work natively in `switch` statements, including the newer pattern-matching switch expressions in Java 17+.

The interviewer asking this question wants to know if you see enums as a tool for modeling closed sets of behavior — not just named constants.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java enums aren't named integers — they're full classes where each constant is a singleton instance with its own fields, methods, and interface implementations.

**Why they're more powerful than constants**
- Each constant is a singleton created once at class loading; constructors are implicitly private, so the instance set is fixed at compile time
- Compare with `==`, not `equals()` — both work, but `==` is null-safe and faster for singletons
- Use `EnumSet`/`EnumMap` for collections — bit-vector and array-backed, faster than `HashSet`/`HashMap`

**The strategy pattern without a class hierarchy**
- Define an `abstract` method in the enum and override it per constant: `PREMIUM { public double applyDiscount(double p) { return p * 0.85; } }`
- Adding a new constant forces you to implement the method at compile time — a switch statement would silently ignore new values

**Built-in safety properties**
- Thread-safe: JVM initializes enums during class loading, once, safely
- Serialization-safe: deserialization returns the existing singleton, not a new duplicate — no broken `==` identity

I recommend enums wherever you have a closed fixed set of options with associated behavior — not just as a replacement for integer constants.

sections.title: Four Types of Nested Classes — And the Hidden Reference That Causes Memory Leaks
sections.content:
Java has four kinds of classes you can define inside another class: **static nested**, **non-static inner**, **local**, and **anonymous**. The single most important distinction is whether the nested class holds a reference to the enclosing object — because that reference is invisible in your source code but very real in the heap.

A **non-static inner class** automatically captures a reference to the enclosing instance. You can't create one without an outer object: `outer.new Inner()`. This means the inner instance keeps the outer instance alive — if the inner object is stored in a cache, a listener list, or any long-lived data structure, the outer object can never be garbage collected. This is the **most common source of memory leaks** in Android development and a frequent interview topic.

A **static nested class** has no such reference. It's essentially a regular top-level class that happens to live inside another class's namespace for organizational purposes. It can access the outer class's `private` static members but knows nothing about any specific outer instance. When you don't need access to the outer object's fields, static nested is always the safer choice.

sections.title: Four Nested Class Types Compared
sections.content:
The key differences are about **where** they can be declared, **what** they can access, and **whether** they hold a reference to the outer instance.

| Type | Declared where | Has outer reference? | Can access outer's instance fields? | Typical use case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Static nested | Inside class, with `static` | No | No — only static members | Helper class, Builder pattern, Map.Entry |
| Non-static inner | Inside class, no `static` | Yes (implicit `Outer.this`) | Yes — all fields including private | Iterator implementations, event handlers |
| Local | Inside a method body | Yes (if non-static method) | Yes, plus effectively final local variables | One-off logic scoped to a single method |
| Anonymous | Inline, no class name | Yes (if in non-static context) | Yes, plus effectively final locals | Callbacks, listeners, Comparator before Java 8 |

The **effectively final** restriction on local and anonymous classes exists because the local variable lives on the stack and the inner class object lives on the heap. Java copies the variable's value into the inner class at creation time — if the variable could change afterward, the copy would be stale. Making it effectively final guarantees the copy is always correct.

Since Java 8, **lambdas have replaced most anonymous class usage** for functional interfaces. But anonymous classes are still necessary for abstract classes and interfaces with multiple methods — lambdas only work when there's exactly one abstract method to implement.

- **Lambdas replaced anonymous classes for functional interfaces (Java 8+)** — anonymous classes still needed for abstract/multi-method interfaces.

sections.title: Java Serialization: Powerful, Dangerous, and Mostly Replaced
sections.content:
Java serialization converts an object graph into a byte stream and back. Implement `Serializable` — a marker interface with no methods — and the JVM handles the rest. It traverses every field, serializes referenced objects recursively, and rebuilds the entire graph during deserialization.

The mechanism has a property that most developers don't realize: **deserialization bypasses constructors entirely**. The object is recreated from bytes without calling any constructor, which means validation logic, default values, and invariant checks in your constructors never run. This is both a source of bugs (fields that should have defaults end up null) and a security vulnerability (attackers can craft byte streams that create objects in invalid states).

`serialVersionUID` is a version number that ties serialized bytes to a specific class structure. If you don't declare one, the JVM computes it automatically from the class's fields, methods, and interfaces. **Add a field, and the auto-generated UID changes** — meaning previously serialized objects can't be deserialized, throwing `InvalidClassException`. Declaring it explicitly (`private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L`) lets you control compatibility across versions.

`transient` marks fields that should be excluded from serialization — passwords, cached computations, thread-local state. These fields get their type's default value (`null`, `0`, `false`) after deserialization. In practice, most modern Java services have moved to JSON serialization via Jackson or Gson, which is human-readable, language-agnostic, and doesn't carry Java serialization's security baggage.
