sections.title: Java Serialization vs JSON: Why the Industry Moved On
sections.content:
Java's built-in serialization served its purpose but has fundamental problems that modern alternatives avoid.

| Aspect | Java Serialization (`Serializable`) | JSON (Jackson/Gson) |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Binary — not human-readable | Text — inspectable and debuggable |
| Cross-language | Java-only | Language-agnostic |
| Constructor usage | Bypassed — object created from bytes directly | Calls constructor or factory method |
| Security | Known attack vector — crafted byte streams can execute arbitrary code | Safer — no code execution from parsing |
| Versioning | `serialVersionUID` — fragile across class changes | Schema evolution via `@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)` |
| Performance | Fast for Java-to-Java | Slightly slower due to text parsing, but negligible for most use cases |
| Field exclusion | `transient` keyword | `@JsonIgnore` annotation |

Java serialization still has **legitimate use cases** — session replication in servlet containers, deep cloning of complex object graphs, and inter-JVM communication in distributed systems like Hazelcast or Spark. But for API communication, data storage, and configuration, JSON or Protocol Buffers are the modern standard. The Java team itself has acknowledged this — Project Amber discussions have explored deprecating `Serializable` in future Java versions.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Deserialization bypasses constructors** — object rebuilt from bytes; validation in constructors doesn't run; use `readObject()` instead.
- **`serialVersionUID` prevents `InvalidClassException`** — without it, adding any field changes the auto-generated UID and breaks deserialization.
- **`transient` for sensitive or non-serializable fields** — passwords, connections, and caches should not be serialized.
- **`Externalizable` gives full control at full cost** — you write every read/write call manually.
- **Prefer JSON (Jackson) or Protobuf** — language-agnostic, human-readable, no known RCE vulnerabilities.

**The thing most people miss**
- Deserialization bypasses constructors completely — the object is rebuilt from bytes with no constructor call
- Validation logic, default values, invariant checks: none of them run
- This is both a bug source and a security vulnerability — crafted byte streams can create objects in states your constructors would never allow

**`serialVersionUID` — version compatibility**
- Auto-generated UID is computed from the class structure; add a field and the UID changes
- Previously serialized objects throw `InvalidClassException` on deserialization

**`transient` and `static`**
- `transient` excludes a field — passwords, caches, thread-local state; comes back as null/0/false

sections.title: Interfaces With No Methods — How Java Signals Capability Without Behavior
sections.content:
Before Java had annotations, the language needed a way to tag classes with metadata — to say "this object can be serialized" or "this object can be cloned" without defining any actual behavior. The solution was the **marker interface**: an interface with zero methods, used purely as a type tag that the JVM checks via `instanceof` at runtime.

The three classic examples are `Serializable` (this object can be serialized), `Cloneable` (this object can be cloned), and `Remote` (this object can be called remotely via RMI). None of them declare a single method. They exist purely as **type tags** — the JVM's serialization mechanism checks `if (obj instanceof Serializable)` before proceeding, and `Object.clone()` checks `if (this instanceof Cloneable)` before allowing the copy.

The question interviewers really want answered is: **why not use annotations instead?** Java added annotations in Java 5, and markers like `@FunctionalInterface` and `@Override` serve similar tagging purposes. The key difference is that marker interfaces **define a type** — you can use `Serializable` in a method signature: `void send(Serializable data)`. This gives you compile-time type checking that annotations can't provide. An annotation on a class can only be checked at runtime via reflection.

However, annotations are more flexible — they can carry values, they don't pollute the type hierarchy, and they can be placed on methods, fields, and parameters, not just classes. In modern Java, **annotations have won** for new features. Marker interfaces remain relevant mainly because `Serializable` and `Cloneable` were designed before annotations existed, and backward compatibility keeps them alive.

sections.title: Marker Interfaces vs Annotations: When Each Approach Wins
sections.content:
Both serve as metadata about a class, but they operate at different levels of the type system.

| Aspect | Marker Interface | Annotation |
|---|---|---|
| Defines a type? | Yes — can be used in method signatures, generics | No — only metadata, checked via reflection |
| Compile-time enforcement | Yes — `void save(Serializable s)` rejects non-Serializable at compile time | No — `@Serializable` would only be checked at runtime |
| Can carry data? | No — no fields or methods | Yes — `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)` carries values |
| Applies to | Classes and interfaces only | Classes, methods, fields, parameters, packages |
| Type hierarchy impact | Adds to the interface hierarchy — shows in `getInterfaces()` | No hierarchy impact — metadata only |
| Modern preference | Legacy — `Serializable`, `Cloneable`, `Remote` | Standard — `@Override`, `@FunctionalInterface`, `@Deprecated` |

The **practical guideline** is straightforward: if you need compile-time type restriction ("this method only accepts objects that have this capability"), a marker interface is the right tool. If you need metadata that doesn't affect the type system — or if you need to tag methods, fields, or parameters — use an annotation. In modern codebases, the annotation approach covers the vast majority of cases.

sections.content:
- **Marker interfaces = type tags checked via `instanceof`** — `Serializable`, `Cloneable`, and `Remote` are the classic three.
- **`Cloneable` without overriding `clone()` throws `CloneNotSupportedException`** — the most useless marker; use copy constructors instead.
- **Annotations replaced markers for most use cases** — `@FunctionalInterface`, `@Override`, custom `@Auditable` annotations.
- **Marker interfaces enable compile-time enforcement** — `List<? extends Serializable>` enforces at compile time; annotations cannot.
- **For new code: prefer annotations** — unless you need compile-time method parameter type constraints.

sections.content:
Marker interfaces are interfaces with no methods — pure type tags the JVM checks at runtime via `instanceof`. `Serializable`, `Cloneable`, and `Remote` are the classic three.

**How they work**
- `ObjectOutputStream.writeObject()` checks `obj instanceof Serializable` before proceeding
- `Object.clone()` checks `this instanceof Cloneable` — otherwise throws `CloneNotSupportedException`
- Note: `Cloneable` doesn't declare `clone()` — that method lives in `Object`; the design is widely criticized

**Marker interfaces vs annotations — the real comparison**
- Marker interfaces define a type: `void send(Serializable data)` gets compile-time enforcement
- Annotations can only be checked at runtime via reflection — no compile-time parameter restriction
- But annotations are more flexible: carry values, apply to methods/fields/parameters, don't pollute the type hierarchy

**Modern Java chose annotations**
- `@Override`, `@FunctionalInterface`, `@Deprecated` — all annotations, not marker interfaces
- `Serializable` and `Cloneable` remain because they predate annotations (Java 1.1) and backward compatibility keeps them alive

I recommend annotations for new code unless you specifically need compile-time method parameter type enforcement that only marker interfaces can provide.

sections.title: How One Constraint Still Separates Interfaces From Abstract Classes After Java 8
sections.content:
Java 8 blurred the line between interfaces and abstract classes when default methods arrived — suddenly interfaces could carry method implementations, not just declarations. A lot of developers came away thinking the distinction no longer mattered. It does, and one constraint is the reason: **interfaces cannot hold instance state**.

An interface defines a contract — what an object can do. `Comparable`, `Serializable`, `Cacheable`: capabilities you bolt onto a class. A class can implement as many as it needs, because each adds only behavior, not fields. Abstract classes model what something *is*. They carry fields, constructors, and shared logic that subclasses inherit as part of their identity.

The is-a vs can-do framing helps for most decisions. A `Dog` is an `Animal` — abstract class. A `Dog` can be `Comparable` — interface. But the underlying rule is simpler: the moment you need a base type to hold mutable instance fields (a timestamp, a connection, a counter), interfaces are off the table. They can only hold `public static final` constants.

The other enduring difference is multiple inheritance. A class can implement any number of interfaces but extend only one class. This is why public APIs (Spring, Jakarta EE) almost always expose interfaces as their contract — consumers need to extend their own class hierarchies, not the library's. Abstract classes appear in the *implementation*, not in the public surface.

sections.title: Feature Comparison: What Each Abstraction Can and Cannot Do
sections.content:
The critical differences are about **state ownership**, **inheritance model**, and **access control** — not just syntax.

| Feature | Abstract Class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Instance fields | Yes, any access modifier | Only `public static final` constants |
| Constructors | Yes (called via `super()`) | No |
| Method implementations | Any method can have a body | `default` and `static` methods only (Java 8+) |
| Multiple inheritance | Single extends only | A class can implement many interfaces |
| Access modifiers on methods | `protected`, `private`, etc. | `public` (or `private` for helpers, Java 9+) |
| State mutation | Can hold and mutate state | Stateless by design |
| When to use | Shared base implementation, template method pattern | Capability contract, API surface, multiple inheritance |

The **state ownership** row is the one that resolves most decisions. The moment your base type needs to hold mutable fields — a timestamp, a connection, a counter — interfaces are off the table. Everything else Java 8 brought to interfaces (default methods, static methods) didn't change this fundamental constraint. If you need shared state, you need an abstract class. If you only need shared behavior, an interface with default methods works.

sections.title: Decision Checklist: When to Use Which
sections.content:
Follow this decision tree when choosing between an abstract class and an interface:

**Step 1 — Do you need instance state?** If the base type must hold mutable fields (a counter, a connection, a timestamp), you need an abstract class. Interfaces can only hold `public static final` constants.

**Step 2 — Do you need constructor logic?** If initialization requires validation, resource allocation, or computed defaults that subclasses inherit, use an abstract class. Interface fields are initialized inline and cannot run constructor logic.

**Step 3 — Does the type represent identity or capability?** If it represents *what something is* (Animal, Vehicle, Notification), use an abstract class. If it represents *what something can do* (Serializable, Comparable, Cacheable), use an interface.

**Step 4 — Do consumers need multiple inheritance?** If a class needs to combine behaviors from multiple sources, those sources must be interfaces. Java allows only single class inheritance, so abstract classes are exclusive — choose wisely.

**Step 5 — Will third-party code extend this type?** Interfaces are safer to evolve: adding a `default` method doesn't break existing implementations. Adding an abstract method to an abstract class forces every subclass to implement it, which is a breaking change for external consumers.

In practice, most modern Java APIs (Spring, Jakarta EE, Micronaut) prefer interfaces for public contracts and use abstract classes internally for shared implementation. The `AbstractList` and `AbstractMap` classes in the JDK are canonical examples: the public contract is `List`/`Map` (interface), and the abstract class provides skeletal implementations that concrete classes like `ArrayList` build on.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **IS-A vs CAN-DO** — abstract class = identity (what it is); interface = capability (what it can do).
- **Abstract class can have state and constructors** — instance fields, non-public methods, constructor logic; interfaces cannot.
- **Java 8+ default methods blurred the line** — interfaces can have implementations; the decision now hinges on shared state.
- **One `extends`, many `implements`** — interfaces compose; abstract classes constrain to a single hierarchy.
- **Prefer interface for backward-compatible evolution** — adding `default` is non-breaking; adding `abstract` breaks every subclass.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In Java, both abstract classes and interfaces let you define behavior that subclasses or implementing classes must provide — but they serve different design intents. An abstract class defines what something IS, supporting shared state and partial implementation. An interface defines what something CAN DO, as a pure contract that any class can fulfill regardless of its inheritance hierarchy.

**Abstract class — IS-A, shared state**
- Can hold instance fields, constructors, and methods with any access modifier
- Use when subclasses share mutable state (a counter, a timestamp) or initialization logic
- Template method pattern: parent defines the algorithm skeleton, children override specific steps

**Interface — CAN-DO, pure contract**
- No instance fields (only `public static final` constants)
- A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class — interfaces compose; abstract classes don't
- `Comparable`, `Serializable`, `Runnable` describe capabilities, not identity

**How Java 8 changed the picture**
- Default methods let interfaces carry method bodies — the decision is no longer "do I need implementations?"
- The real question: do you need shared mutable state or a constructor? If yes → abstract class
- Adding a `default` method to an interface is backward-compatible; adding an `abstract` method to an abstract class breaks every existing subclass

I recommend reaching for an interface first; add an abstract class only when state or constructor logic is genuinely needed.

sections.title: The API Evolution Problem That Made Default Methods Necessary
sections.content:
Before Java 8, adding a method to an interface broke every class that implemented it. When the JDK team wanted to add `stream()` and `forEach()` to `Collection` and `Iterable`, they faced an impossible choice: break millions of lines of existing code, or never evolve the API. Default methods solved this — they let interfaces provide a fallback implementation that existing classes inherit automatically, with no changes required.

A **default method** has a body prefixed with `default`. Any class that implements the interface gets the method for free; if it wants a different behavior, it overrides like any other method. A **static method** in an interface is a utility method scoped to the interface namespace — it can't be overridden and is called as `InterfaceName.method()`.

The JDK makes heavy use of both. `List.sort()`, `Collection.stream()`, `Iterable.forEach()` are all default methods added in Java 8. `List.of()`, `Map.of()` are static factory methods on interfaces. These additions doubled the useful API surface of core collections without requiring any migration from existing code.

The wrinkle interviewers probe is the **diamond problem**: what happens when a class implements two interfaces that both declare a default method with the same signature? Java forces the class to override and explicitly choose — ambiguity is a compile error, not a runtime surprise. This keeps default methods safe to use while enabling multiple inheritance of behavior.

sections.title: When Two Interfaces Disagree: How Java Forces You to Resolve the Conflict
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Default methods = backward-compatible API evolution** — how Java added `Collection.stream()` without breaking every existing implementation.
- **Static methods = utility methods namespaced to the interface** — `List.of()`, `Map.of()`; not inherited by implementing classes.
- **Diamond problem forces override** — two interfaces with same default method: compiler demands explicit `InterfaceName.super.method()`.
- **Resolution order: concrete class wins > sub-interface wins > must override** — in that priority order.
- **Default methods with state = wrong tool** — if your default method needs instance state, it belongs in an abstract class.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Default and static methods in interfaces were added in Java 8 to extend interfaces without breaking every class that implements them — the motivation was adding `Collection.stream()` to millions of existing codebases.

**Default methods:**
- Provide a method body in the interface using the `default` keyword
- Existing implementations automatically inherit the behavior without any code changes
- Classic example: `Collection.stream()` was added as a default — no custom collection broke

**Static methods:**
- Utility methods namespaced to the interface — `List.of()`, `Map.of()`, `Comparator.naturalOrder()`
- Not inherited by implementing classes; called on the interface name directly

**Diamond problem:**
- Two interfaces with the same default method: the compiler forces you to override it
- Resolve with `InterfaceName.super.method()` to explicitly choose which default to use
- Resolution rules: concrete class wins > sub-interface wins > must override if still ambiguous

I recommend default methods for backward-compatible API evolution, not as a way to add implementation inheritance — if your default method needs state, it belongs in an abstract class.

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding in Java?
questions.title: Method Overloading vs Method Overriding in Java
questions.direct_answer: Overloading means multiple methods in the same class share a name but differ in parameter types or count — resolved at compile time. Overriding means a subclass provides its own implementation of a method inherited from the parent — resolved at runtime via dynamic dispatch. Overloading is compile-time polymorphism; overriding is runtime polymorphism.

sections.title: Why the Compiler Handles One and the JVM Handles the Other
sections.content:
Both overloading and overriding let you write the same method name multiple times — which is why they're often confused. But they operate at entirely different stages of execution.

**Overloading** is a compile-time decision. Multiple methods share a name but differ in parameter types or count. When you call `calculate(5, 3)`, the compiler looks at the argument types at the call site, picks the matching signature, and bakes that choice into the bytecode. There's nothing left to decide at runtime — the method is already chosen before the program runs.

**Overriding** is a runtime decision. A subclass provides its own implementation of a method from the parent class with the exact same signature. The JVM checks the actual type of the object at runtime and dispatches to the right implementation. You might hold an `Animal` reference that's actually a `Dog`, and `animal.speak()` calls Dog's version, not Animal's — dynamic dispatch picks based on what the object *is*, not what it's *declared as*.

The distinction explains two important follow-ups: why changing only the return type can't create an overload (the compiler can't distinguish calls by return type, only by argument types), and why static methods can't be overridden (they're resolved at compile time by declared type — the JVM never gets a chance to check the runtime type).

sections.title: Feature Comparison: Compile-Time vs Runtime Polymorphism
sections.content:
The fundamental difference is **when** the method is chosen — at compile time (overloading) or at runtime (overriding).

| Aspect | Overloading | Overriding |
|---|---|---|
| Where | Same class (or inherited) | Subclass replaces parent method |
| Resolved at | **Compile time** | **Runtime** (dynamic dispatch) |
| Method signature | Same name, **different parameters** | Same name, **same parameters** |
| Return type | Can differ freely | Must be same or covariant (subtype) |
| Access modifier | No restriction | Cannot be more restrictive than parent |
| Exceptions | No restriction | Cannot throw broader checked exceptions |
| `static` methods | Can be overloaded | Cannot be overridden — only **hidden** |
| `final` methods | Can be overloaded | Cannot be overridden |
| `private` methods | Can be overloaded | Not inherited, so not overridable |
| `@Override` annotation | Not applicable | Strongly recommended — catches typos |

The **static method hiding** row is the most important interview trap. If you declare `static String species()` in both `Animal` and `Dog`, calling `animal.species()` on a `Dog` object returns Animal's version — because static methods are resolved by the declared type, not the runtime type. This is hiding, not overriding, and it catches developers who assume polymorphism applies to static methods.

sections.title: The @Override Annotation: Why It's Not Optional in Practice
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Overloading = compile-time, overriding = runtime** — compiler resolves overload by parameter types; JVM resolves override by actual object type.
- **Cannot overload by return type alone** — parameter list must differ; return type change without parameter change is a compile error.
- **Static methods are hidden, not overridden** — dispatch uses declared reference type, not the actual object type.
- **`@Override` is mandatory** — without it, a typo silently creates a new method instead of overriding the parent.
- **Covariant return types are allowed** — child override can return a more specific type than the parent declared.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Overloading and overriding are Java's two forms of polymorphism — they differ in *when* the method is selected: compile time vs runtime.

**Overloading (compile-time):**
- Multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists (types or count)
- Compiler picks the matching overload at the call site based on argument types
- Cannot overload by return type alone — the parameters must differ

**Overriding (runtime):**
- Subclass provides its own implementation of an inherited method with the exact same signature
- JVM uses dynamic dispatch: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak()` calls Dog's version at runtime
- Rules: same or wider access, covariant return types allowed, fewer checked exceptions allowed

**Gotchas:**
- Static methods are **hidden, not overridden** — dispatch uses the declared type, not the actual object type
- Always use `@Override` — without it, a typo silently creates a new method instead of overriding

I recommend thinking of overloading as convenience (multiple ways to call the same behavior) and overriding as specialization (subclasses customizing inherited behavior).

sections.title: Why a static Variable Is Shared State and a static Nested Class Doesn't Leak Memory
sections.content:
Every member in Java lives at one of two levels: instance or class. **Instance members** belong to a specific object — each `new Dog()` gets its own copy of every field. **Static members** belong to the class itself — one copy, shared by every instance, accessible without creating any object.

That single distinction has consequences that interviewers probe. **Static variables are shared mutable state** — a `static int counter` incremented from multiple threads without synchronization is a race condition. **Static methods have no `this` pointer** — they can't access instance fields, which is why `main()` must be static (no object exists when the JVM starts). **Static blocks run once when the class first loads** — before any constructor, in textual order, and an exception here permanently breaks the class with `ExceptionInInitializerError`.

**Static nested classes** are self-contained: unlike non-static inner classes, they don't hold a hidden `Outer.this` reference. A non-static inner class holds that reference even when you don't need it, which prevents the outer object from being garbage collected — a memory leak that's easy to miss.

`static` also powers the static factory method pattern. `List.of()`, `Optional.empty()`, `BigInteger.valueOf()` can cache instances, return subtypes, and carry descriptive names that constructors can't provide.

sections.title: The Memory Leak You Get When You Choose Inner Class Instead of Static Nested Class
Static Initialization Order and Its Traps
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`static` = belongs to the class, not to any instance** — one copy shared across all objects; accessible without instantiation.
- **Static variables are shared state** — thread safety concern; concurrent writes need `AtomicInteger` or `synchronized`.
- **Static methods have no `this`** — cannot access instance fields; foundation of factory patterns (`List.of()`, `Optional.empty()`).
- **Static blocks run once at class loading** — if a static block throws, the class gets `ExceptionInInitializerError` permanently.
- **Default to static nested class** — avoids the hidden `Outer.this` reference that prevents GC of the enclosing instance.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`static` means the member belongs to the **class**, not to any instance — one copy shared across all objects, accessible even when no instances exist.

**Static variables:**
- Shared across all instances — useful for counters, constants, shared configuration
- Thread-safety concern: concurrent writes need `AtomicInteger` or `synchronized`

**Static methods:**
- No `this` pointer — cannot access instance fields directly
- Foundation of factory patterns: `List.of()`, `Optional.empty()`, `BigInteger.valueOf()`
- `main()` is static because no object exists when the JVM starts

**Static blocks:**
- Run once when the class is first loaded, before any constructor, in textual order
- Useful for one-time setup like loading native libraries
- If a static block throws, the class gets `ExceptionInInitializerError` and becomes permanently unusable

**Static nested classes:**
- A non-static inner class secretly holds a reference to the enclosing instance — can prevent GC
- Static nested class is self-contained — no hidden reference, no memory leak risk

questions.title: Immutability in Java — How and Why
questions.direct_answer: An immutable class is one whose state cannot change after construction. To create one: make the class final, make all fields private and final, don't provide setters, perform defensive copies of mutable fields in the constructor and getters, and initialize all fields via the constructor. Immutability matters because immutable objects are inherently thread-safe, safe as HashMap keys, and eliminate entire categories of bugs.

sections.title: final Fields Alone Don't Make a Class Immutable — The Trap Is Mutable Objects Inside Final References
sections.content:
The most common mistake when creating immutable classes is declaring all fields `final` and assuming the job is done. `final` prevents **reassignment** — the reference can't point to a different object. But if the referenced object itself is mutable (like a `List` or `Date`), anyone holding a reference to it can modify its contents, corrupting the supposedly immutable instance.

A truly immutable class requires four things: the class must be `final` (preventing subclasses that could add mutable state), all fields must be `private final`, there must be **no setters or mutation methods**, and mutable objects must be **defensively copied** both when received in the constructor and when returned from accessors.

Immutability matters because it provides **thread safety without synchronization** — if state can't change, concurrent reads are inherently safe. It also makes objects safe as HashMap keys (the hash can't change after insertion) and enables safe sharing and caching. String, Integer, and all wrapper types in Java are immutable for exactly these reasons.

Java records handle most of this automatically — fields are `private final`, the class is `final`, and `equals()`/`hashCode()` are generated. But records don't defensively copy mutable components, which is the one thing you still need to handle manually.

sections.title: The Complete Checklist: Four Requirements for True Immutability
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`final` freezes the reference, not the object** — a `final List` can still have elements added; true immutability requires more.
- **Four requirements: `final` class, `private final` fields, no setters, defensive copies** — the defensive copy is the step most people miss.
- **`List.copyOf()` vs `Collections.unmodifiableList()`** — `copyOf()` is independent; `unmodifiableList()` wraps the original so changes leak through.
- **Records handle 3 of 4 automatically** — `final` class, `final` fields, no setters; they do NOT defensively copy mutable components.
- **Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe** — no synchronization needed; safe to share across threads freely.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The trap with immutable classes is that `final` prevents reassignment, not mutation — a `final List<String>` can still have elements added or removed.

**Four requirements for true immutability:**
- Make the class `final` — prevents mutable subclasses from adding state or overriding methods
- All fields `private final` — prevents direct access and reassignment after construction
- No setters or mutation methods — prevents internal state changes
- **Defensive copies** for mutable components — the step most people miss

**Defensive copying:**
- `this.tags = tags` means the caller's list and your internal field share the same object — mutating one mutates both
- `this.tags = List.copyOf(tags)` creates an independent unmodifiable copy — modifications from neither side affect the other
- `Collections.unmodifiableList(tags)` is insufficient — it wraps the original, so changes to the original still leak through

**Records and immutability:**
- Records handle `final` class, `final` fields, and no setters automatically
- Records do **not** defensively copy mutable components — add `Order { items = List.copyOf(items); }` in the compact constructor

I recommend `List.copyOf()` over `Collections.unmodifiableList()` for defensive copies — it provides true independence from the original.
